records.text: Ooh, look where that piece landed. It's poking at several targets at the same time, which makes it a fork. Sneaky!
Hmm, notice anything off? One of the other side's pieces can now jump on several targets in one go. That's a fork waiting to happen.
Psst, there was a fork tucked inside another move! One piece could have poked at a bunch of targets together. This move walked right by that clue.
See that piece on the line? It can't budge, because the king is sitting right behind it. Frozen in place by a pin!
Suspicious line alert! A pin is on offer for the other side: one piece could get frozen in front of its king.
Psst, another move had a pin to the king tucked inside it. That piece would have been frozen on its line. This move never noticed.
Skewer spotted! The front piece is under fire, and when it scoots out of the way, the one hiding behind it gets exposed.
Hmm, two pieces are lined up like ducks. The other side can skewer them: if the front one shuffles aside, the back one could be exposed.
Ooh, a skewer was hiding in another move. Chase the front piece off the line, and the one behind would have been exposed. Missed clue!
Who was guarding that? This defender, that's who. Take the defender away, and the thing it guarded is suddenly on its own.
Interesting! Somebody's defender is a sitting target now, and if it goes, whatever it was guarding goes unprotected too.
Hmm, a different move could have snatched a defender and left its job undone. This one let that little trick slip away.
Peek at the back rank! The king is stuck behind its own pieces with nowhere to run, and this move goes right for it.
Clue spotted: the king's own pieces are blocking its escape hatch. Now the other side has a shot at a back-rank mate.
A back-rank mate was hiding here! The king was trapped by its own pieces, and this move tiptoed past it.
Watch that little pawn go. It's scampering off to the far end, and once it reaches the last rank, it turns into a brand-new piece!
Hmm, one of their pawns is sneaking toward the last rank. That's a promotion chance for them.
Ooh, a stronger move would have opened the way for a pawn to promote. This move kept that door shut.
Sneaky! One piece slides out of the way, and surprise, the piece behind it was aiming all along. That's a discovered attack, sneaking up out of nowhere!
Something's hiding behind one of their pieces. If that piece wanders off, the one behind it gets to attack. A discovered attack, theirs for the taking.
A discovered attack was tucked inside another move! One piece could have stepped aside to unveil the attacker behind it. This move kept the curtain closed.
Two threats popping out of this one move! Both threats are going to need answers.
Hmm, one move from the other side could now carry two threats. A double attack like that means answering twice.
A stronger move could have poked at two things at once. Ooh, that double attack stayed hidden this time.
Shoo! The defender gets lured away from its post, and its old post has nobody minding it. Lured right off, the classic deflection!
Look at that defender, working so hard. The other side can now lure it off its job, a deflection, and leave its post empty.
A deflection was waiting in another move, a defender just begging to be lured off. That deflection is still sitting there, unused.
Who's guarding that piece? Nobody! So it gets taken. Simple as that.
Wait, there was an unguarded piece up for grabs with another move. Nobody was watching it, and this move left it alone.
Hmm, who's guarding that piece now? Nobody, and the other side can just take it.
Case file: who was protecting that piece? Just one real defender, and this move walked it away. The piece it abandoned is now up for grabs.
Here's the clue: the opponent's last move made a threat. This move never dealt with it, so a piece can be captured.
The capture looks tasty, but then comes the recapture, and it takes back something bigger. Peek at both halves of the trade first.
Hop! A minor piece jumps out of its starting spot. Out of bed and into the game!
Another move could have developed a minor piece, getting it off its starting square.
The rook found an open file! Not a single pawn on it, of either color.
A different move could have handed a rook an open file, empty of pawns of both colors.
Ooh, the rook found itself a semi-open file. None of its own pawns there, but at least one enemy pawn is still loitering.
With another move, a rook would have landed on a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns while an enemy pawn lingers.
Look closely at that pawn! Not one enemy pawn blocks it, on its file or the two next to it. It's a passed pawn.
Another move would have made a passed pawn, with not one enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or the files next to it.
Sneak, sneak, the passed pawn moves up again. Closer and closer to the last rank.
A different move could have nudged the passed pawn closer to the last rank.
Aw, this pawn is all by itself now, no friendly pawn on the files on either side. Poor little isolated pawn.
Another move would have left a pawn isolated, with no friendly pawns on the files on either side of it.
That piece was standing around unguarded, and now it has a buddy watching its back. A defender!
With another move, that unguarded piece would have had company. Nobody likes standing alone.
Hmm, this piece is left without a single guard. Suspicious! Though unguarded doesn't mean it can actually be won.
With another move, a piece would have been left unguarded. That on its own wouldn't prove it could be won.
The king just got a new escape hatch, a legal square it didn't have before.
A different move could have given the king a new legal square to step to.
Whoosh, the king castles! King and rook hop past each other in one quick move.
Another option was castling, moving the king and rook together in a single move.
Snap! One side's bishop pair is gone after this capture. Now one side only has a bishop on one color of square.
Another move would have nabbed a bishop, leaving the other side without its pair.
Two pawns of one color, piled up on the same file. They're doubled!
A different move would have left doubled pawns, two of one color piled up on a single file.
Big clue. After this move, forced checkmate is on for the other side. Let's trace the attack and find where the defense gave out.
Wait a second! A forced checkmate was right there, and this move missed it. Rewind and sniff out that finish.
Ooh, a gift that isn't really a gift! The other side can take the material, but in the line we checked, the trick keeps working.
Every other move we checked was losing. This sneaky little move was the only one keeping the position playable. Tricky!
Only this move keeps the advantage alive; every other one we checked was losing. Case closed on that one.
Something's up with the reply: the other side can snatch something straight away. What would they grab?
Clue: the top reply checks the king! Nothing else matters until the king is out of trouble.
Hmm, why does the engine prefer a different move here? Set its move up on the board and see how the replies change.
What's this move costing? A bit of value against the engine's best, and the reply holds the clue.
Case report: strong. Even under the engine's magnifying glass, it gives away almost nothing.
Sound as can be. The engine likes a different one a bit more, but this keeps most of what the position had.
The human-move model says this is a natural move to play. But the engine finds a stronger one, and the reply shows why. Sneaky trap!
The human-move model never saw this one coming. But the engine still rates it strong. A sneaky little gem!
Only one move we checked kept the position playable, and this wasn't it. The human-move model says that defense was a tricky find.
The engine's best, and a tricky find, according to the human-move model and the alternatives we checked. Remember this one!
You sniffed it out! This move is why the position holds, and the human-move model and the alternatives we checked say it was a tricky defense to spot.
The human-move model expects this move, and it's the engine's best too. Everybody agrees for once!
The human-move model thinks this is a natural move, and the engine calls it strong, though its top pick is something else.
Psst, the clock was nearly out of time before this move. That's a clue too.
Zoom! That move came quickly, with time still left.
That was a long, long ponder. The clock ticked for a good long while.

Bye-bye, opening book! No more map from this point on.
Look who's back! The earlier setback is behind us, and this move makes the position playable again.
We're back to playable after that earlier setback! The other side's errors helped us along.
The opponent's last move left a little gap, and this move pounces!
The opponent's last move left a little gap. This move didn't spot it.
Hey, I've seen this clue before! This exact trouble already turned up in an earlier moment of this game. Let's put those moments next to each other.
That piece left unguarded earlier has a defender again. Patched up!
Where did it all go wrong? Nowhere big! Just lots of small concessions adding up, and this is one more of them.
The advantage never slipped away, right up to the recorded win. Mystery solved, and nicely handled!
This issue keeps turning up! It's lurking in your other saved games too. Line them up and look for the pattern.
Checkmate, and every escape hatch is shut. All wrapped up!

A draw, so nobody wins this one, but there are still earlier decisions worth poking at.

By the end of the saved line, the side that made this move has less material than it started with.

On to the next one. What changed? Have a peek.

Phew, the king is out of check thanks to this move.
The pawn made it to the last rank and turns into a new piece!
The pawn gets to the last rank, turns into a new piece, and gives check too!
Up to the last rank, a promotion, and checkmate! Not a single legal escape for the king.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and with that same move, its own king escapes the check.
Snatch! A piece gets captured.
A capture, and it's check too!
A capture, and that's checkmate! The king has nowhere left to wriggle.
A capture that rescues the king from check. Two jobs in one!
Snatch and promote! The pawn captures as it lands on the last rank.
Capture, promotion and check, all packed into one pawn move!
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and it's checkmate! The king has nowhere left to wriggle.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and with that same move, its own king escapes the check.

The king castles, and that's checkmate! That enemy king is locked in tight, no legal moves left.
One piece pokes at several targets, then grabs one of them. The fork comes out ahead in material here, net.
That capture is off-limits for that piece. It's stuck on a pin, and leaving the line would expose its own king.
The piece under attack is stuck in a pin against its king, so it can't just run away. Whatever it does, the king has to stay hidden behind it.
The defenders are stuck in pins against their king, so nobody can take back. The line shown ends up with extra material, too.
Stepping off the line would leave its king exposed, so the pinned piece just has to sit there. Before the moves run out, it's captured anyway.
Out of the way goes the front piece, and the one that was hiding behind it is captured along the line.
The king gets checked and has to hop off the line. Then the very same attacker scoops up whatever was behind it.
Step one: the lone defender is snapped up. Step two, later on: whatever it was guarding gets snapped up as well.
The defender gets tempted away, and its old charge gets captured right after.
The blocking piece moves out of the way, and the newly opened line lets another piece capture.
One piece steps aside, and surprise, there's check from the piece that was hiding. Peekaboo!
Double check, ooh! Two attackers on the king at the same moment, so only a king move can answer.
The moving piece attacks once and reveals another attack behind it. This time, the second attacker gets its prize.
A promotion, and in this example that side comes out with more material, net.
That piece had no guard, so off it goes. The side that grabbed it is ahead in material by the end of this example.
Here's a sneaky one. Until the opponent's previous move, the attacking piece sat in a relative pin, and that move let it go. The target never moved, and in the line shown, it gets captured.
That marked reply is fair game for the other side. Pop it on the board for a closer look!
Before moving, hunt for any piece of yours that could be taken without a useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, sniff out any enemy piece that's missing a guard.
Look for forcing moves where one piece can poke at two valuable targets.
Thinking of moving a pinned piece? Peek at what's behind it first. Is it the king, or something worth more?
An attack might go right through the first target. Is something valuable hiding behind it?
Planning to swap off a defender? First find out what it's protecting right now.
When a blocking piece moves, peek at every line it opens behind it.
Sniff out a move with two threats packed inside. Checks count, and so do lines that just opened up!
Thinking of moving a back-rank defender? First spot where the king could run.
How many moves does the pawn need to promote? Count them, then check every forcing pawn push.
Before a defender moves, check which pieces it's guarding. Those are the ones it would abandon.
Count what you capture, then count what the recapture takes back.
Could a forcing exchange tempt a defender away from another job? Check that.
